Epigramma
ΦΩΤΙΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΙΑΡΧΟΥ ΚΩΝΣΤΑΝΤΙΝΟΥΠΟΛΕΩΣ, ἄλλοι δέ φασιν
ΛΕΟΝΤΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΟΥ
Ἔρωτα πικρόν, ἀλλὰ σώφρονα βίον ὁ Κλειτοφῶντος ὥσπερ ἐμφαίνει λόγος· ὁ
Λευκίππης δὲ σωφρονέστατος βίος ἅπαντας ἐξίστησι, πῶς τετυμμένη κεκαρμένη τε
καὶ κατηχρειωμένη, τὸ δὴ μέγιστον, τρὶς θανοῦσ' ἐκαρτέρει. εἴπερ δὲ καὶ σὺ
σωφρονεῖν θέλῃς, φίλος, μὴ τὴν πάρεργον τῆς γραφῆς σκόπει θέαν, τὴν τοῦ λόγου
δὲ πρῶτα συνδρομὴν μάθε· νυμφοστολεῖ γὰρ τοὺς ποθοῦντας ἐμφρόνως.
thought_title: The story shows bitter love but a chaste life
orientation: The author opens the epigram by attributing it to Photius or Leo and then states what the story of Clitophon displays.
pass_a_gloss: Epigram. Of Photius patriarch of Constantinople, but others say of Leo the Philosopher. The story of Clitophon, as it were, displays bitter love but a chaste life. And the most chaste life of Leucippe amazes everyone, how, having been beaten and having been shorn and having been abused, and, the greatest thing indeed, having died three times, she endured. If you too wish to live chastely, my friend, do not look at the incidental spectacle of the writing, but attend first to the movement of the story. For it escorts those who love wisely to the bridal chamber.

pass_b_english: The story of Clitophon displays bitter love, but a chaste life. Leucippe's most chaste life amazes everyone: beaten, shorn, abused, and—greatest of all—having died three times, Leucippe endured. If you too wish to live chastely, my friend, do not dwell on the incidental spectacle of the writing, but learn first the movement of the story. For it escorts those who love wisely to the bridal chamber.

problems.fix: Unify to 'attend first to' or 'learn first' throughout.
